0.0.n: お + the stem of 答える + なさい makes a firm command, despite the polite-looking お.

0.2.n: This is Homura’s family name, placed before her given name in Japanese.

0.3.n: ほ is the first part of the given name ほむら, not a separate word here.

0.4.n: むら completes the given name ほむら; it does not mean village here.

1.0.n: This is a name written in katakana, commonly used for foreign names.

1.1.n: を marks Marguerite as the one to be returned.

1.2.n: 返す becomes 返して before いただきます, politely framing the other person’s action as a favor, but conveying firm intent here.

2.0.n: あの comes before a noun and points to someone or something distant or already known to both speakers.

2.1.n: 子 literally means child, but あの子 can refer familiarly to a girl or young person.

2.2.n: を marks the girl as the person being called by a name.

2.3.n: 勝手 criticizes choosing a name to suit yourself without permission.

2.4.n: な connects 勝手 to 名前 so it describes the kind of name.

2.5.n: 名前 is modified by 勝手な, showing disapproval of the chosen label.

2.6.n: で marks the name used when addressing or referring to her.

2.7.n: 呼ぶ becomes 呼ばないで, a direct request for someone not to do the action.

0.tip: なさい gives a firm instruction; it is not a gentle request.

1.lit: Marguerite, I will receive the favor of you returning.
1.tip: ていただきます sounds polite but here announces what the speaker intends to have the other person do.

2.lit: That girl, by an arbitrary name, don't call.
2.tip: ないで at the end asks someone not to do something.
